newsitem.title: GERMANY: German marine insurers see flat 1996.
newsitem.headline: German marine insurers see flat 1996.

text.p: German marine insurers have said they expect a "dramatic decrease" in ocean hull insurance for 1996, as well as reduced income from carriers' liability.

"Only in cargo insurance and smaller additional lines will we have a small rise," Dietrich Gundermann, chairman of the marine committee in Germany's property and casualty insurers' federation Verband der Schadenversicherer (VdS), told Reuters.
In 1995, marine insurers had lifted gross premium income by 0.3 percent to 3.07 billion marks.
"In ocean hull, we are losing a lot of business to the London market and to Scandinavian insurers," Gundermann said.
"They are undercutting us by up to 50 percent. In London, they now offer three-year contracts, which the insurer cannot terminate, even after a loss. I think this is impossible business behaviour."
German companies play only a small role in marine hull insurance, with gross income in 1995 of just 138 million marks.
"In 1996, we see another decline by 30 percent," said Gundermann. There would be underwriting losses. "At today's prices, no-one can earn any money."

Only in hull insurance for pleasure craft was the situation better. Here, the industry reported growth of seven percent to 106 million marks in 1995 and said this year's income would grow by five percent.
This line also made an underwriting profit last year and is likely to do so again this year, said Gundermann.
In cargo, the largest marine line with 1.34 billion marks in 1995, modest economic growth is leading to sluggish growth in 1996, Gundermann said. "But I believe we will see a rise again in 1997."
Prices were weakening in cargo, too, so that underwriting losses for 1996 are probable, following break-even after settlement gains for 1995.

For carriers' liability, Gundermann expects another drop, following a 2.4 percent fall to 523 million marks in 1995. "There are a number of reasons, for example bankruptcies of freight forwarders, but also the merciless competition, which in fact is totally unnecessary."
For the small additional lines, Gundermann forecasts slight rises of the premium income total. In 1995, they rose by 3.8 percent to 815 million marks.
Species insurance caused particular problems. "We see more and more valuables being lost in transit, including those sent by post, and more attacks on security transportation firms."
